challenges.headline: Editing the total directly
challenges.premise: Users should be able to edit the reported total itself, as if it were a stored field.
challenges.alternative: Record each change as a separate, attributed adjustment line (amount, account, period, reason, author) that makes the total add up. The underlying entries stay untouched and the correction can be reversed. A replaced value would be built only if there is a specific, approved reason to accept a figure that disagrees with its data.
challenges.consequence: A total is an aggregate of entries. Overwriting it makes the report silently disagree with its own source data, defeats reconciliation, and leaves nothing for an auditor to trace. Retrofitting traceability later is expensive.
challenges.recommendation: Get the requester to confirm that adjustment is the intended behaviour, and to name the situations (wrong source figure, late correction, management decision) in which users currently want to change a number, before any design starts.

challenges.headline: Editing without regard to period close
challenges.premise: Totals can be edited whenever a user wants, as a simple edit form.
challenges.alternative: Allow free adjustment only in open periods. After close, route corrections to an adjustment in the next open period by default, and treat re-opening a closed period as a separate, logged, permissioned act that flags prior exports as outdated.
challenges.consequence: Changing a closed or already-exported period invalidates everything sent or filed from it. A plain edit form would let figures move after finance has relied on them.
challenges.recommendation: Ask which periods users actually need to correct in practice, and decide the closed-period path before estimating.

challenges.headline: Building a new export
challenges.premise: The finance team needs a new export built for this feature.
challenges.alternative: The platform already exports to the accounting system. Extending it so that adjustments appear as separate lines, or so that it adds a finance-team view, may cover the need at a fraction of the cost. A new export is justified only if the current one cannot carry the required fields or format.
challenges.consequence: A second export duplicates a format contract that must be kept consistent with the first, and doubles the places where rounding and cut-off conventions can diverge.
challenges.recommendation: Compare the current export's fields, format and recipients with what finance actually asked for, and extend before building.

complexity_reasons: adjustment versus override changes the data model, not a setting
audit trail with no gaps across a shared aggregation layer
period close, restatement and stale-export propagation
export as a versioned contract with a downstream consumer
briefs.cost_driver: adjustment model with audit trail and restatement handling
risks: An override built without a visible marker would make reports stop tying back to the source data, and this would only surface at audit time.
The aggregation layer is shared by every report, export and dashboard, so adding adjustments can shift figures elsewhere, including budget vs. actual.
Permissions (see, adjust, approve, close, scoped by entity) are easy to leave to the end, and segregation of duties may be a compliance requirement.
An export that does not match the consumer's format, rounding or field set will be rejected downstream, and nothing yet states that format.

Almost every substantive answer so far is an assumption: the real reason for editing, the current process and the success criteria are all unknown, so scope could shift materially after the first conversation.

opportunities.text: Make adjustment an engine on the aggregation layer (entry, reason, approval, reversal), so every derived figure can be corrected the same way.
Build the audit trail as a shared service rather than a feature-local log, so who-changed-what is recorded consistently for adjustments, period re-opens and exports.
Version and retain every export snapshot, enabling retrieval of exactly what was sent and later stale-export flagging.
Per-client configuration of approval circuits and export field mappings, once at least two clients show different needs.

next_steps: Hold a short discovery session with a controller and the finance recipient to settle adjustment versus override, the reasons users edit today, and how corrections reach finance now.
Compare the existing accounting export with what finance needs, and decide whether to extend it or build a new one.
Settle the rights model (see, adjust, approve, close, entity scoping) and the closed-period path, then write acceptance scenarios around tie-out, audit and closed periods.
Build the first release as adjustments in open periods with audit trail and an extended versioned export; defer per-client configurability and restatement automation.

challenges.headline: Editing the total directly
challenges.premise: Users should be able to edit a reported total, as if it were a stored number.
challenges.alternative: Treat the total as read-only and let users enter an adjustment (amount, account, period, reason) that the total is then summed from. The original figure stays visible, and the adjustment can be reversed or approved separately.
challenges.consequence: A true override makes the report silently disagree with its own source entries, breaks reconciliation, and leaves the audit trail with a gap at exactly the figure someone changed.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with Finance that an adjustment model meets the need before any design. Allow an override only if a specific case requires it, and then mark it visibly with author and reason.

challenges.headline: Building before checking existing export
challenges.premise: A new export for the finance team is needed.
challenges.alternative: The platform already exports to the accounting system and reviews and closes periods. Extending that export to include adjusted figures, or switching on an existing correction path, may cover most of the request.
challenges.consequence: A second export path means two definitions of 'the figures' reaching finance, and two formats to keep aligned with the downstream consumer.
challenges.recommendation: Walk through the current export with Finance and write down precisely what it lacks before committing to any new export build.

challenges.headline: Edits ignoring period close
challenges.premise: Users can edit totals whenever they like, as the request states no limits.
challenges.alternative: Allow free adjustment only in open periods. After close, route corrections into the next open period as an adjustment, and treat re-opening as a rare, logged, approved act.
challenges.consequence: Editing a closed period invalidates exports and filings already made, and the restated figures must then be propagated and notified.
challenges.recommendation: Decide the post-close rule with Finance before estimating, since it determines whether a restatement path is in scope.

complexity_reasons: adjustments layered on derived aggregation shared by every report
audit trail that must have no gaps
export as a contract with a downstream consumer
briefs.cost_driver: the adjustment model and its audit trail on top of shared aggregation
risks: The aggregation layer is shared, so introducing adjustments can shift every report, dashboard and export at once. 'Actuals' and 'actuals plus adjustments' must remain separate views.
Segregation of duties and entity-scoped rights are likely to be discovered only at acceptance, forcing rework of permissions.
Exports already sent become stale when a figure changes, and without versioning finance cannot retrieve what was actually sent.
Rounding, cut-off and FX conventions are unstated, so adjusted totals may fail to tie out to the penny.
Nearly every business rule is still unanswered, so any estimate made now is low-confidence.

opportunities.text: Build adjustments as a general attributed, reversible entry type with its own approval, so other corrections can reuse the same mechanism and audit history.
Make exports versioned and retained snapshots, so any figure sent can be reproduced and compared with later restatements.
Reuse the platform's existing approval circuits for adjustment approval rather than building a separate one.

next_steps: Hold a working session with Finance to settle adjustment versus override, post-close behaviour, and who may adjust, approve and close.
Review the existing accounting export and any unused correction capability, and write down the specific gap this request fills.
Confirm whether an audit or compliance obligation sits behind the request, and what an auditor must see per change.
Only then scope a first release limited to open-period adjustments, a basic audit history and a versioned export.

decisions.decision: Seeing, adjusting and closing are treated as separate rights

decisions.tradeoff: More permission design up front, in exchange for avoiding a late rework at acceptance.

decisions.tradeoff: Added build effort now, for a trail without gaps.

briefs.problem: Reported totals sometimes need correcting, and the corrected figures must reach the finance team, but nothing says why totals are wrong today or how corrections are traced.
briefs.solution: A controlled adjustment mechanism on derived period totals, tied to the period lifecycle, with an audit trail, role-based rights and a versioned, retained export that reflects adjustments.
introduces: an adjustment-entry capability (attributed, reasoned, reversible) layered on derived totals
an approval circuit and segregation-of-duties rules for adjustments
a field-level audit trail covering who changed which figure, when, why, and previous vs new value
versioned, retained export snapshots with stale-export detection after a restatement
entity/cost-center scoped rights separating view, adjust and close

challenges.headline: Editing the total itself
challenges.premise: Users should be able to edit the reported totals directly, as if a total were a stored field.
challenges.alternative: Because a total is the sum of underlying entries, a change can be recorded as a separate adjustment line with an author, a reason and an approval, so the total still adds up. Overwriting the displayed value would be the other reading.
challenges.consequence: An overridden value silently stops tying back to its own source data. Finance will then ask for 'actuals' and 'actuals including adjustments' as separate numbers, and an override cannot supply them. It also leaves a gap at audit time.
challenges.recommendation: Agree with the client that every edit is an adjustment entry, not an overwrite, before any design work. If a true override is wanted, require a visible overridden marker with who and why.

challenges.headline: Whether to build editing
challenges.premise: A new edit capability is needed, rather than fixing the cause of the wrong totals or reusing what exists.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has aggregation, period review and close, and an export to the accounting system. If totals are wrong because of bad source data, correcting at the source and re-aggregating may be cheaper. If the cause is late or management corrections, extending the existing period review and export may cover most of the need.
challenges.consequence: Building a parallel edit path and a second export risks duplicating the existing close and export logic, and creates two versions of the truth for finance.
challenges.recommendation: Find out why totals need editing and how finance gets corrected figures today. Check whether the existing export can carry adjusted figures before specifying a new one.

challenges.headline: Editing after period close
challenges.premise: Users can edit totals whenever they notice an error, including in periods that are already closed.
challenges.alternative: Open periods take adjustments directly. For closed periods, a correction can be booked as an adjustment in the next open period, with re-opening kept as a rare, logged, approved act.
challenges.consequence: Mutating a closed period invalidates every export and report already issued from it, and weakens the audit position. Re-opening for routine corrections turns close into a formality.
challenges.recommendation: Decide the closed-period policy with the controller or finance manager before build, because it determines whether restatement handling is in scope.

complexity_reasons: audit trail with no gaps on every figure that moves
interaction with the period lifecycle and restatement of prior exports
adjustment approval and scoped permissions that likely vary by client
changes to the shared aggregation layer ripple to all reports and dashboards
briefs.cost_driver: the adjustment, approval and audit model on derived figures
risks: The shared aggregation layer feeds every report, export and dashboard, so adding adjustments risks changing existing figures unless raw and adjusted views are kept separate.
Prior exports and published reports go stale when a figure moves after they were sent; without versioning and notification, finance may act on outdated numbers.
Segregation of duties and entity-scoped rights are easily missed and then discovered at acceptance testing, requiring rework of the permission model.
The export consumer's format, rounding and encoding rules are unknown, and a mismatch may be rejected downstream.
Cut-off, FX and rounding conventions are unstated; the wrong convention moves money between periods or breaks tie-out to the penny.

opportunities.text: Build the adjustment entry as a general, attributed and reversible record that the period close, budget vs. actual and exports all read, rather than a screen-specific edit.
Extend the existing accounting-system export to carry adjusted figures, with versioned and retained snapshots so a sent export can be retrieved exactly.
Make adjustment approval circuits and export field mappings client-configurable, reusing the platform's existing configurability pattern.

next_steps: Hold a short discovery session with a controller and finance manager to settle: adjustment vs. override, open vs. closed period edits, and why totals need editing today.
Check whether the existing accounting export and period close can carry adjusted figures, and confirm the receiving format and whether sent exports must be retrievable.
Define roles for viewing, adjusting, approving and closing, with segregation of duties and entity scoping, and confirm whether any audit requirement is driving this.
Then estimate and build in this order: adjustment entries with audit trail, approval and period-lifecycle rules, then the versioned export.

decisions.decision: Treat edits as adjustment entries on derived totals, not overwrites (proposed for the client to confirm)
decisions.why: Totals are aggregations of entries, so a traceable adjustment keeps the report tied to its data and supports an audit trail.
decisions.alternative: Replace the displayed total with the typed value.
decisions.tradeoff: More build effort and a second 'with adjustments' view, in exchange for traceability and reconcilability.

decisions.decision: Include an audit trail (who, when, why, previous vs new value) as part of core scope
decisions.why: Financial reporting carries auditability and statutory retention expectations, and retrofitting an audit trail late is expensive.
decisions.alternative: Add the audit trail in a later phase.
decisions.tradeoff: Higher initial effort, in exchange for avoiding gaps at audit time.

decisions.decision: Keep view, adjust and close as separate rights, with the adjuster not approving their own change
decisions.why: Segregation of duties is expected in financial reporting and is hard to add after the fact.
decisions.alternative: A single finance role that can do all three.
decisions.tradeoff: More roles and configuration, in exchange for control and audit defensibility.
